meta.note: Figures copied by hand from official reports (veterinary institutes, food-safety and environment agencies). Each block names its source. Measures differ by country: read the 'measure' field before comparing levels.

NO.name: Norway
NO.source: Norwegian Veterinary Institute, Fish Health Report 2025 (published 2026)
NO.measure: share of the fish at sea that die in the year (count, monthly risks compounded)

causes.note: Share of registered dead fish by main cause, AquaCloud database (408 sea sites, about half of Norway's), not the true prevalence

diseases.note: Number of sites with the disease detected (Veterinary Institute and private laboratories)

highlights: Mortality 14.2 % in 2025, the lowest in five years; 1.72 Mt harvested (+11 %) — fewer losses were part of the big 2025 volumes.
Injuries from handling and delousing are now the first registered cause of death (33.5 %); non-medicinal delousing hit a record 3,918 treatment-weeks (+24 %), linked to warm autumn seas in the south.
Gill disease is the No. 1 problem named by fish health staff; AGD found at 99 sites (40 in 2024), as far north as PA10 and Troms.
ISA up to 18 sites (13), mostly Vesterålen, 7 of them at vaccinated sites; HSMI 167 sites (115), CMS 114 (78), IPN 40 (13) — new IPN variants seem to get past the IPN-resistant (QTL) eggs.
PD keeps falling (44 sites against 100 in 2021); winter ulcer down after a new vaccine (246 sites against 289).
Worst areas: PA4 20.1 %, PA1–2 18.2 %, PA5 17.5 %; PA9 jumped 7 points (ISA outbreaks and a spring algal bloom). Best: PA12–13 9.4 %.
Smolts put to sea fall for a third year: 405 M in 2025, against 462 M in 2022.
Policy: target of about 5 % mortality; a quota on lice-larvae emissions and a mortality levy are being studied.

card.s: first half 5.8 % against 7.3 % (−21 %); September back above last year

why.causes: Injuries from handling and delousing are now the first recorded cause (33.5 % of registered deaths). Gill disease is the No. 1 problem for fish health staff; AGD was found at 99 sites (40 in 2024). Heart diseases HSMI (167 sites) and CMS (114) are up, ISA at 18 sites, IPN three times 2024.
why.worse: Warm autumns in the south bring more lice, so more treatments: a record 3,918 treatment-weeks in 2025. Toxic algae in the south in spring 2026. ISA in Vesterålen even at vaccinated sites. Fewer cleaner fish (18.9 M against 48 M in 2021) means more mechanical and thermal delousing.
why.supply: Better survival carried part of the 2025–26 volumes. But smolts put to sea fell for a third year (405 M) and there are 6 % fewer fish at sea: once mortality stops falling, Norwegian supply flattens. To watch: autumn sea temperatures, spring algae in the south, ISA in the north.

NO.supply_line: Survival kept volumes up; fewer smolts and 6 % fewer fish at sea cap the upside.

events.t: Toxic algae in the south (PO1–2): first-half mortality there rose from 6.1 % to 15.8 %.
End of the southern algal bloom declared.
Fish Health Report 2025: mortality 14.2 %, lowest in five years; injuries from delousing now the first cause.
Half-year mortality 5.8 % against 7.3 %; the north improves sharply (Vestfjorden–Vesterålen 12.3 % → 4.3 %).
Monthly mortality back above last year: warm autumn, lice season (Fiskeridirektoratet register).

CL.name: Chile
CL.source: Sernapesca, Informe Sanitario de Salmonicultura en Centros Marinos, año 2025 (March 2026)
CL.measure: share of the fish put to sea that died, farms harvested in the year (closed cycles, count)
highlights: Closed-cycle mortality of Atlantic salmon 10.1 % in 2025 (11.0 % in 2024); trout 7.2 %, coho 4.7 %. Monthly mortality fell 1.5 % on 2024 while biomass rose 17 %.
SRS (Piscirickettsia salmonis) remains the first infectious killer: 52.8 % of infectious deaths of Atlantic salmon, then tenacibaculosis 31.5 %. Coho dies mostly of HSMI and jaundice syndrome.

Sea lice (Caligus): loads stable in Los Lagos and Aysén; Aysén peaked at 3.6 egg-bearing females per fish (week 42); 211 high-surveillance farms went above 3.0 during 2025, mostly fish near harvest size. Magallanes much lower.
ISA: no outbreak of the virulent variant for the second year running (last in 2023).

Algal blooms (FAN) are the big tail risk: 2016 (about 39,000 t, Los Lagos) and 2021 (7,100 t, Comau fjord and Aysén) — with El Niño, Chile declared a preventive algal-bloom emergency in 15 regions in 2026.

card.s: SRS at Camanchaca, ISA at Izaza and Luchín, and 918 t lost to algae in Magallanes in October; El Niño

why.causes: SRS (Piscirickettsia salmonis) causes 52.8 % of the infectious deaths of Atlantic salmon, then tenacibaculosis (31.5 %). Sea lice (Caligus) force treatments and early harvests. Coho dies mostly of HSMI and jaundice syndrome.
why.worse: Algal blooms are the tail risk — about 39,000 t lost in 2016, 7,100 t in 2021 — and El Niño raises it: Chile declared a preventive algal-bloom emergency in 15 regions in 2026. The virulent ISA came back in Aysén in September–October 2026, the first cases since 2023.
why.supply: Chile harvested early in 2025–26 and has less fish in the water. ISA, sea lice and El Niño put the risk for 2027 on the downside; an algal bloom like 2016 would remove several percent of world supply in a few weeks.

CL.supply_line: Less fish in the water, ISA back, El Niño: the risk is on the downside.

events.t: Invermar: about 283 t of salmon (around 10 % of one farm's biomass) killed by low oxygen.
Salmones Camanchaca: SRS outbreaks at several sites, US$2.8 M of exceptional mortality in the first quarter; SRS again at two sites in the second quarter.
65 farms listed for sea lice above the threshold in the third quarter, against 43 in an average quarter (Sernapesca).
ISA (HPR5a) at Izaza, Salmones Camanchaca, ACS 20 in Aysén: zoning, harvest of the fish finished on 14 October.
ISA (HPR3a) at Luchín, Cermaq Chile, ACS 30A — no link with Izaza according to Sernapesca; positive cages harvested by 23 October.
Sernapesca health report 2025: closed-cycle mortality of Atlantic salmon 10.1 % (11.0 % in 2024).
Magallanes: a Leptocylindrus minimus algal bloom killed 918 t at Multi X's Taraba sites (concessions 43A/43B); Sernapesca authorised early harvest, with strong El Niño alerts.
No national mortality rate for 2026 yet: Sernapesca publishes it once a year (the 2026 report is due around March 2027). Until then, losses are known event by event.

IS.name: Iceland
IS.source: MAST (Icelandic Food and Veterinary Authority), Ársskýrsla dýralækna fisksjúkdóma 2025
IS.measure: dead fish tonnes ÷ average biomass at sea (MAST dashboard)

smolts_to_sea_m.note: salmon smolts put in sea cages (MAST report, table 4)

highlights: About 4.7 M salmon died at sea in 2025 (East fjords 2.3 M, Westfjords 2.4 M) and about 650,000 were culled — while harvest rose 17.6 % to 64,400 t.

Winter: cold sea and storms → net abrasion, winter ulcers (Moritella viscosa, Tenacibaculum) and Parvicapsula; part of the early-2025 losses came from smolts put to sea too late, into cold water, in autumn 2024 (MAST referred one case to the police).
Berufjörður (East): summer losses from algal blooms (Thalassiosira, Leptocylindrus) hurting gills, plus Costia and jellyfish.

Westfjords: heart and muscle inflammation (HSMI, virus PRV) weakening fish, sea lice (13 medicinal and 19 warm-water treatments), and kidney disease (BKD) — three sea areas infected at the end of 2025, spread probably by boats and gear.
ISA: no virulent case since 2022 (30 positive samples for the harmless HPR0 variant out of 11,957).
Smolts put to sea jumped to 19.5 M in 2025 (13.0 M in 2024): the base of Iceland's growth in 2026–27.
2026: over one million salmon died in September alone, mostly jellyfish in Reyðarfjörður (Kaldvík).

card.s: January–September better than 2025, but jellyfish killed over 1 M fish in September

why.causes: Winter: cold sea and storms rub fish against the nets, then winter ulcers (Moritella viscosa, Tenacibaculum) and the gill parasite Parvicapsula. Summer: algae and jellyfish in the East fjords. Westfjords: heart and muscle inflammation (HSMI), sea lice and kidney disease (BKD).
why.worse: Smolts put to sea too late, into cold water (MAST referred one case to the police); BKD spreading between sea areas with boats and gear (three areas infected at the end of 2025); one treatment-vessel failure killed most of a pen in August 2025.
why.supply: Growth is real — smolts put to sea rose from 13.0 M to 19.5 M in 2025 and harvest is up by almost half in 2026 — but losses swing month to month: a single jellyfish or cold spell can remove a tenth of a fjord's stock.

IS.supply_line: Smolts up to 19.5 M: growth is real, losses are volatile month to month.

events.t: Dead fish at 13.6 % of the average biomass, against 17.9 % a year earlier (MAST).
Over one million salmon died in the sea cages, mostly jellyfish in Reyðarfjörður (Kaldvík) — the third-highest month since 2020.
MAST annual report 2025: 4.7 M salmon died at sea and about 650,000 were culled; BKD in three Westfjords areas at year end.

FO.name: Faroe Islands
FO.source: Bakkafrost annual reports (no yearly public health report from the Faroese authority, Heilsufrøðiliga Starvsstovan)
FO.measure: Bakkafrost Faroes, share of fish dying in the year (company figure)
highlights: Bakkafrost Faroes mortality 4.29 % in 2025, the lowest of the major basins (6.6 % in 2024, 11.56 % in 2018).
Sea lice under control with low counts (0.27 adult females per fish in 2025) and long fallow periods (13–20 weeks).
ISA flares up now and then and is handled by culling: Bakkafrost culled about 180,000 salmon after an ISA detection at a Faroese site in May 2024.
Bakkafrost has reported pasteurella bacteria (pasteurellosis) in the Faroes.

card.s: no exceptional mortality in Q1–Q3; no ISA since May 2024, no AGD reported

why.causes: Low losses: Bakkafrost Faroes 4.3 % in 2025. ISA flares up now and then and is handled by culling (about 180,000 salmon in May 2024); pasteurella bacteria have been reported.
why.worse: Few: sea lice under control (0.27 adult females per fish in 2025) and long fallow periods between cycles.
why.supply: Health is not the constraint in the Faroes: volumes follow licences and Bakkafrost's plans.

FO.supply_line: Health is not the constraint; volumes follow licences.

events.t: Bakkafrost Faroes: 7.3 % mortality; main causes handling and treatments, seals, CMS, HSMI, gill health.
ISA at Bakkafrost A-19 Vágur (2 pens, about 180,000 fish culled); site harvested early, 2,000–3,000 t off the 2024 harvest. Last ISA case found.
Bakkafrost Faroes: 6.6 % mortality; causes handling (stocking, delousing), seals, wounds, ISA, CMS. Mowi Faroes: 15 % of sites above the lice limit.

Bakkafrost Faroes: 4.3 % mortality, the lowest since 2019; causes wounds (winter ulcers, mechanical) and handling. No thermal delousing any more. Mowi Faroes: no incident-based mortality cost, 3 % of sites above the lice limit.
Bakkafrost Faroes: no exceptional mortality cost in Q1, Q2 or Q3; survival 90 days after transfer about 97.5 % in Q3; harvest 75.0 kt in nine months.

No ISA and no AGD outbreak reported in 2025–2026. AGD, CMS, HSMI and BKD are known to be present in the Faroes (Seafood Watch 2022); HFS publishes lice counts every two weeks by site but no database of disease cases.

kpis.d: stocked minus harvested (HFS data via Seafood Watch); Bakkafrost 10.3 %, Hiddenfjord 4.9 % in 2021

GB.name: Scotland
GB.source: SEPA farm returns (deaths and biomass) and Fish Health Inspectorate mortality reports (Marine Directorate)
GB.measure: dead fish tonnes ÷ average biomass at sea (SEPA)
highlights: Scotland loses far more than Norway or the Faroes: about 28,000 t of dead fish in 2025, 22.5 % of the average biomass (29–30 % in 2022–23).
Gills are the first cause in the farms' reports to the Fish Health Inspectorate (complex gill disease, AGD, plankton and jellyfish), then bacterial disease.
Warm autumns make it worse: amoebic gill disease losses in Shetland pushed Scottish Sea Farms into the red.
Early harvests of small fish to limit losses (Bakkafrost Scotland) act like mortality on supply.

card.s: Bakkafrost harvests small fish early (Q2–Q3, 3.0 kg), Scottish Sea Farms gill incidents and early harvests

why.causes: Gills come first in the farms' reports to the Fish Health Inspectorate — complex gill disease, AGD, plankton and jellyfish — then bacterial disease. About 28,000 t of dead fish in 2025, 22.5 % of the average biomass.
why.worse: Warm autumns on the west coast and in the Northern Isles; exposed sites; treatments of weak fish. Incidents can wipe out a third of a farm in a cycle (Fada 38.9 %, Fiunary 32.4 % in 2026).
why.supply: Biology, not licences, sets Scottish supply. The sign to watch is early harvesting of small fish: it inflates supply for a few weeks, then leaves a hole — Scottish Sea Farms cut its 2026 volume from 43,000 to 40,000 t.

GB.supply_line: More fish in the pens, but gill incidents and early harvests keep cutting forecasts.

events.t: Bakkafrost Scotland: Pasteurella skyensis at Portree, 900 t harvested early at 2.3 kg.
Campaigners call on Scottish farms to scale back after record mortalities.

Bakkafrost Scotland: biological problems in one batch of bought-in smolts at Sgian Dubh and Ardyne; harvest down 55 % to 3,145 t, DKK 31–32 M of exceptional mortality. The company does not name the disease.
Bakkafrost Scotland harvests the two sites out early: 4,537 t at only 3.0 kg on average, DKK 42 M of exceptional mortality (33.5 M from the sites emptied); the effect runs into Q4.
Scottish Sea Farms: gill incidents at Fada (38.9 % over the cycle), Fiunary (32.4 %) and Tanera (over 30 %); sites emptied early.
Scottish Sea Farms cuts its 2026 harvest guidance by 3,000 t to 40,000 t.
Mowi Scotland harvested a third less than a year earlier.
Mowi Scotland: incident-based mortality cost €4.2 M in Q3 (€2.9 M a year earlier), put down to warmer sea water; 2026 guidance kept at 74,000 t.
Fish Farm Production Survey 2025: 197,836 t produced (+3 %); 68.8 % of the 2023 smolt year class reached harvest, against 61.8 % for the 2022 class.

kpis.d: early harvest of two sites; DKK 42 M exceptional mortality

CA.name: Canada
CA.source: DFO (Fisheries and Oceans Canada) carcass classification for British Columbia; provinces of Atlantic Canada for ISA
CA.measure: British Columbia: monthly mortality % of fish on site, compounded over the year (DFO)
highlights: British Columbia: open-net farms in the Discovery Islands have been closed and the remaining licences end in 2029; the DFO data show the causes month by month — 'environmental' (algae blooms, low oxygen) first, 42 % of deaths in 2025.

Atlantic Canada has no mortality rate published like BC's. What exists: ISA detections (CFIA), New Brunswick's fish-health notices by bay management area, drugs and pesticides used by site (DFO), and Newfoundland's compulsory public report of any loss above 10 % of a site's fish.
ISA is back hard in New Brunswick: 14 detections from February to August 2026, after 10 in 2025, 7 in 2024 and 2 in 2023 — the most since 2021 (29).

Newfoundland, 2025: Mowi Canada East's head called it the worst year of his 40-year career — about 400,000 salmon dead at three Harbour Breton Bay sites in August (warm water, low oxygen), more losses in July and December (sea lice).

Treatments show the pressure: New Brunswick used 5.6 t of the antibiotic oxytetracycline in 2024 (68 kg in 2023), a sign of bacterial outbreaks; azamethiphos baths against sea lice continue in Newfoundland (444 kg in 2024).

atlantic_events.cause: sea lice: residual effects of the autumn 2025 infestation

atlantic_events.site: Harvey Hill East, Harvey Hill South, Broad Cove (Harbour Breton Bay)
atlantic_events.fish_note: fish at the sites affected; about 400,000 reported dead
atlantic_events.cause: not stated: warm, low-oxygen summer; Mowi spoke of a rare ocean event

sources_extra: Newfoundland — aquaculture incident reporting (public report of losses above 10 %)

card.s: BC first half 13.6 % against 7.9 %; ISA in New Brunswick at its highest since 2021

why.causes: British Columbia: "environmental" causes — algal blooms and low oxygen — were 42 % of the deaths in 2025 (DFO). Atlantic Canada: ISA keeps coming back (New Brunswick), and warm, low-oxygen summers kill fish by the hundreds of thousands in Newfoundland.
why.worse: Warming coastal waters; sea lice and their treatments in Newfoundland; storms that stop harvesting. Atlantic Canada has no published mortality rate — only ISA detections, treatments and Newfoundland's reports of losses above 10 % of a site.
why.supply: BC open-net farming ends in 2029 anyway; losses speed up the decline. In the Atlantic, Mowi expected 12,000 t instead of 17,000 t in 2026 because of die-offs, and is selling the business to Cooke.

CA.supply_line: BC winds down by 2029; ISA and summer die-offs weigh on the Atlantic.

events.t: 14 ISA detections in New Brunswick (CFIA), after 10 in the whole of 2025.
Cooke agrees to buy Mowi Canada East (NB, PEI, NL) for $225 M; Mowi expected 12,000 t instead of 17,000 t this year.
British Columbia: mortality 13.6 % in the first half, against 7.9 % a year earlier (DFO).
Newfoundland: Mowi Canada East calls 2025 the worst year in 40 years — about 400,000 salmon dead in August, sea-lice losses in December.

AU.name: Tasmania
AU.source: EPA Tasmania (mortality waste by month), NRE Tasmania / EPA debrief of the 2025 event
AU.measure: dead fish tonnes (mortality waste) compared with the year's production
highlights: About 20,100 t of salmon died in 2025 — roughly 30 % of the 68,000 t produced in 2024/25; February 2025 alone 6,300 t.

Main trigger: Piscirickettsia salmonis (SRS, the bacterium behind most infectious deaths in Chile), present on the east coast since at least 2021 and in the south-east since 2023, now endemic and not eradicable.

Made worse by marine heatwaves (east Tasmanian waters warm almost four times faster than the world average), algae and jellyfish blooms; vaccine protection is partial; density was ruled out as the cause.
2026 is not back to normal: 14,900 t from January to September, and March–June 34 % above 2025; the emergency permit for the antibiotic florfenicol was suspended in February 2026.
Risk season is the austral summer (December–April): high losses in early 2027 are the base case.

why.causes: Piscirickettsia salmonis (SRS) — the bacterium behind most infectious deaths in Chile — was the main trigger of the 2025 event in the D'Entrecasteaux Channel (Huon, Tassal). Present on the east coast since 2021 and in the south-east since 2023, now endemic and not eradicable.
why.worse: Marine heatwaves: east Tasmanian waters warm almost four times faster than the world average, and outbreaks follow the summer temperature peak. Algae and jellyfish blooms, partial vaccine protection, and the emergency permit for the antibiotic florfenicol suspended in February 2026. Density was ruled out as the cause.
why.supply: About 20,100 t died in 2025, some 30 % of the year's production. Heavy losses each austral summer (December–April) are now the base case, not the exception.

AU.supply_line: SRS endemic, antibiotic permit suspended: heavy losses each austral summer.

events.t: Macquarie Harbour: about 1,150 t of dead salmon removed in six months (peak 314 t in January), government RTI release.
66 'elevated mortality' events reported statewide (40 in Huon / D'Entrecasteaux Channel, 12 Storm Bay, 7 Macquarie Harbour).
Tassal: 89.2 % survival in marine pens (88.3 % in freshwater), against 91 % in 2023.
EPA: 9,200 t of dead salmon in January–March 2026, about a third less than the 2025 event.
The emergency permit for florfenicol is suspended by the veterinary medicines authority.
March–June 2026: 8,300 t dead, 34 % more than in 2025.
Official debrief of the 2025 event: P. salmonis the main trigger, response plan missing.

notes.measures: Norway, Chile and the Faroes count fish; Scotland, Iceland and Tasmania weigh them (dead tonnes against biomass or production). A tonnage measure gives more weight to large fish lost late in the cycle, so it usually runs above a count measure. Compare trends within a country rather than levels across countries.
